source.title_on_document: Style, sentiment, and quality of undergraduate writing in the AI era: A cross-sectional and longitudinal analysis of 4,820 authentic empirical reports

supplement.where: Appendices 1-8 are printed in the PDF (pp. 13-18). Further material is on OSF: https://osf.io/ezc37/?view_only=af6e614bf90a464283dc6ad37743120d (p. 13, Code/data availability).
supplement.holds: PDF appendices hold the interrupted-time-series model outputs (Appendix 1), longitudinal cohort models (Appendix 2), prompts, topic distribution, score and feedback figures, the AI-assistance classification, pre-registration deviations, and submission counts. OSF holds analysis code, per-report derived statistics (reports and feedback themselves are not shared), the pre-registration, word-count and word-frequency plots, marking criteria, sample feedback, and a DeepSeek-r1 rewrite analysis not reported in the paper (pp. 3, 4, 11, 13).

paper_design_summary: The authors analyze 4,820 empirical reports written by 2,000 psychology undergraduates at the University of Warwick from 2016 to 2025, comparing reports submitted before and after ChatGPT's launch with interrupted time series mixed models and two cohort-level longitudinal comparisons. Outcomes are the prevalence of eight ChatGPT-associated words, seven formality features (including within-report lexical diversity, MTLD), sentiment, marker grades, and marker feedback on clarity. In an exploratory analysis, GPT-3.5-Turbo and GPT-4o mini rewrite all 3,033 pre-ChatGPT reports sentence by sentence, and the rewrites are compared with the student originals.

studies.label: Warwick Psychology Student (WPS) corpus, pre- vs post-ChatGPT (cross-sectional interrupted time series and Special Cohort longitudinal analyses)

assignment.what_was_assigned: No AI assistance was assigned. The observational corpus compares reports submitted before and after ChatGPT’s launch.
assignment.quote: the observational nature of this study prevents us from concluding that these changes were causally driven by GenAI.
assignment.prereg_locator: pp. 2-3, Sections 1.4 and 2: Stage 2 was preregistered in early April 2025, after Stage 1 analyses of the 2016-2024 reports and before receipt of the 2025 reports. pp. 17-18, Appendix 7, items 1-2: switching to interrupted time series analysis and computing counterfactual models/predictions were departures from the preregistration. The entire analysis was therefore not preregistered. Registration is referenced via OSF: https://osf.io/ezc37/?view_only=af6e614bf90a464283dc6ad37743120d (the registration itself was not independently opened).

participants.who: Psychology undergraduates at the University of Warwick who submitted empirical reports (1st-year replication, 2nd-year extension, final-year dissertation) between 2016 and 2025; 4,820 reports, 17.2 million word tokens; 3,033 reports pre-ChatGPT (2016-2022) and 1,787 post-ChatGPT (2023-2025). Special Cohort 1 N = 155, Special Cohort 2 N = 164.
participants.quote: We conducted pre-registered analyses of 4820 empirical reports authored by 2000 psychology undergraduates (2016–2025)
participants.locator: p. 1, Abstract; p. 2, Section 1.3; p. 3, Section 2.4; p. 17, Appendix 6; p. 18, Appendix 8

ai_tool.name_model: ChatGPT and other generative AI tools, use not observed (no student disclosed AI use)
ai_tool.how_used: AI use is inferred from submission timing (2023 onward = post-ChatGPT); the department allowed limited declared use from September 2023, and no student declared use (pp. 2, 3).

task.description: Empirical psychology lab reports (about 2,000 words in year 1, 4,000 in year 2, 4,000-8,000 for the final-year dissertation), written as graded coursework under unchanged instructions.

outcomes.name: Lexical diversity (MTLD) of each report, cross-sectional interrupted time series
outcomes.question: none
outcomes.measure_detail: Measure of Textual Lexical Diversity (McCarthy & Jarvis, 2010), koRpus R package, factor size 0.72; range of unique words within one report, controlling for length. It is within-text vocabulary variety, not similarity across writers (p. 3-4, Section 2.6).

contrasts.control_arm: Pre-ChatGPT reports (2016-2022) and the counterfactual trend fitted to them

outcomes.name: Prevalence of eight ChatGPT-associated words (proportion of reports containing each word)
outcomes.question: none
outcomes.measure_detail: Target words: crucial, comprehensive, intricate, pivotal, delve, underscore, utilise/ze, align (with inflections); control words conclude, technical. Proportion of reports per submission year containing each word, compared with a counterfactual mixed model fitted to 2016-2022 (pp. 3, 5).

contrasts.reported: In 2024, prevalence exploded to 0.226 ... exceeding the 95 % confidence intervals of the projected trend [0.035, 0.181]; in 2025 prevalence declined by 17.2 % (vs. 2024) to 0.188, just below the upper bound of the projected trend [0.039, 0.193]

outcomes.name: Sentiment of each report (syuzhet lexicon, normalised by unique words)
outcomes.question: none
outcomes.measure_detail: Bag-of-words sentiment, syuzhet R package and lexicon, summed over unique words and divided by the number of unique words (p. 4, Section 2.7). Not a creativity score.

contrasts.control_arm: Pre-ChatGPT reports (2016-2022) and the counterfactual trend fitted to them

outcomes.name: Report grade (100-point scale, marked by PhD students or faculty)
outcomes.question: none
outcomes.measure_detail: 1st-year reports marked by PhD students, 2nd-year by one faculty member, final-year by two faculty who agreed a score; 2016-2017 final-year scores not retrievable (p. 3, Section 2.3; p. 4, Section 2.8). Overall quality, not a creativity rating.

contrasts.control_arm: Pre-ChatGPT reports (2016-2022) and the counterfactual trend fitted to them

studies.label: GPT-rewritten matched corpora vs pre-ChatGPT student originals (exploratory)

participants.who: Corpus: all 3,033 pre-ChatGPT student reports (10.9 million word tokens) and their sentence-by-sentence rewrites by GPT-3.5-Turbo (11.3 million tokens) and GPT-4o mini (9.6 million tokens). No person received AI help.
participants.quote: we asked two GPT models—GPT-3.5-Turbo (version: 0125) and GPT-4o mini (version: 2024-07-18)—to rewrite all the pre-ChatGPT reports (N = 3033)

ai_tool.name_model: GPT-3.5-Turbo (0125) and GPT-4o mini (2024-07-18) via Microsoft Azure OpenAI Service, temperature 0.7
ai_tool.how_used: The model rewrote each sentence of a student report with the prompt "Rewrite each sentence to improve clarity, coherence, and academic tone." (pp. 4-5).

task.description: Sentence-level rewriting of pre-ChatGPT empirical psychology reports.

outcomes.name: Prevalence of the eight ChatGPT-associated words, GPT rewrites vs student originals
outcomes.question: none
outcomes.measure_detail: Mean proportion of reports containing each target word. Numeric rewrite-versus-original comparisons for MTLD are shown only in Fig. 2A (p. 7); qualitative MTLD comparisons also appear in Sections 3.2 and 4.2 (pp. 6-7, 11). Clausal-density comparisons are printed in Section 3.2 (p. 8): pre-ChatGPT student originals M = 2.11, GPT-4o mini M = 2.08 (p < .001, Cohen’s d = 0.11), and GPT-3.5-Turbo M = 1.69 (p < .001, Cohen’s d = 1.17). Section 4.2 (p. 11) instead prints 1.68 for the GPT-3.5 rewrite mean; this source discrepancy is unresolved. Sentiment comparison is reported as ps < 0.001, ds > 0.77 (p. 9, Section 3.3).

contrasts.reported: MGPT-3.5 = 0.453 for, MGPT-4o-mini = 0.447, compared to the pre-ChatGPT student originals (M = 0.069)

eligibility.reason: S1 is observational: 4,820 reports by 2,000 unique students are compared across submission periods; AI assistance was not assigned and no student disclosed AI use (p. 2, Sections 1.3-1.4; p. 3, Methods). The student count meets the 50-person criterion. The outcomes measure lexical markers, linguistic style, sentiment, and academic quality, without a qualifying creativity, novelty, originality, or across-writer diversity outcome (pp. 3-4, Sections 2.5-2.8). MTLD measures vocabulary variety within one report, not diversity across people. S2 compares automated rewrites with student originals and assigns no people to AI help; its style and sentiment comparisons also fall outside the creative-work scope (pp. 4-5, Section 2.9; pp. 6-9, Sections 3.2-3.3). Creativity and epistemic diversity are proposed for future research (p. 12, Sections 4.5 and 5). Under creativity-codebook.md, Sections 1, 3 and 6, neither study qualifies for core or context evidence.

one_line_finding: In 4,820 Warwick psychology reports (2016-2025), post-ChatGPT reports became more formal and positive, with within-report lexical diversity (MTLD) at 84.71 in 2025 vs a projected 72.98 (Post-ChatGPT trend B = 7.115, p < 0.001) and ChatGPT-associated words peaking at 0.226 prevalence in 2024, while grades did not shift (trend p = 0.725) (pp. 5, 13-14, Appendix 1).
